analysis.one_liner: Bans states from outlawing any FDA-approved contraceptive.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with six Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states from banning any contraceptive drug or device that the FDA has approved, licensed, cleared, or authorized. It carves out protections: states can still regulate the practice of medicine and pharmacy, and no provider or entity can be forced to supply contraception against its religious or moral beliefs. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and to its Health Subcommittee, where it stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use contraception — especially in states that have moved to restrict reproductive health care after abortion rules were returned to the states — would gain a federal guarantee that no state can outlaw an FDA-approved contraceptive drug, biological product, or device. Pharmacists and prescribers would also gain a clearer federal floor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Contraception users, especially in restrictive states

how_it_helps.text: No state may establish, implement, or enforce any ban on the prescription, provision, or use of a contraceptive drug, biological product, or device that the FDA has approved, licensed, cleared, or otherwise authorized for contraception.
The preemption reaches bans on the prescription, provision, or use of contraception, so it covers the supply chain from prescriber to patient, not just the product itself.

analysis.who_pays: State governments would lose the power to ban FDA-approved contraceptives, and any state or local entity that sought such a ban would be stopped. Manufacturers of contraceptive products would face no new cost; the bill imposes no fees, mandates, or funding.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly preserves any state law protecting the right of an entity to opt out of providing contraception on religious or moral grounds, so a pharmacy or health system could still refuse to stock or dispense a contraceptive that a state cannot ban.

The bill does not preempt state authority to regulate the practice of medicine and pharmacy, so states could still use licensing, prescribing, and dispensing rules to make some contraceptives harder to obtain in practice.

For readers who prioritize state authority, overriding state law on any health product is a real cost even when the goal is access; the bill uses federal preemption, a tool its own party often objects to in other health contexts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The guarantee is real but narrower than the title suggests. Because the bill preserves religious and moral opt-outs and leaves states free to regulate medicine and pharmacy practice, it blocks outright bans while leaving many practical routes to restriction open. The cost is a loss of state control over health regulation, which some consider significant and others consider exactly the point.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Stephanie Bice introduced the Access to Safe Contraception Act of 2023 in the House on May 18, 2023.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and to the committee's Subcommittee on Health the next day.
Six Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The action history records no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill would have prohibited states from banning any FDA-approved contraceptive, while preserving religious and moral opt-outs and state authority over medical and pharmacy practice.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new protection, because the bill never moved. States retained full authority over contraceptive policy, and any interest opposed to a federal floor on contraceptive access avoided a floor vote on the question. Patients in states restricting contraception got no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States kept full control; nothing changed for patients

for.name: Rep. Stephanie Bice
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair, Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction, referred it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, so the bill had one-party sponsorship; whether it would have drawn Democratic support on the floor was never tested because it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill guarantees that no state can ban any FDA-approved contraceptive product, protecting the market for these makers in restrictive states. The interest runs alongside patients': both want the products available.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and health providers with religious or moral objections
industries.note: The bill preserves any state law protecting an entity's right to opt out of providing contraception, so objecting providers keep their exemptions. Patients in areas dominated by opting-out providers could still face reduced access.

States would lose the power to ban FDA-approved contraceptives but keep authority over medical and pharmacy practice and over religious and moral opt-out laws. The cost falls on states seeking bans, not on taxpayers.
